question: Why do you want to become a teacher?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific motivation for teaching itself, not just a general love of a subject or a vague wish to help children.

bullets: Name a concrete moment or experience that pointed you toward teaching
Distinguish teaching from adjacent roles like tutoring or youth work
Show the motivation is about the classroom and pupils, not just the subject
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started running a weekly homework club at my old primary school as part of a volunteering scheme, and I noticed how much I looked forward to the moment a concept finally clicked for a child who had been stuck for weeks. That feeling of watching understanding actually form in front of you is what pulled me toward teaching rather than just tutoring on the side. I have kept volunteering there for two years now because I want to get better at that exact skill, not just repeat the same session. Teaching feels like the only path where that becomes the actual job, every day, for a whole class.

commonMistakes: Saying only that they love their subject with nothing about pupils
Giving an answer that could describe any caring profession
No evidence of actual time spent with children or young people
followUps: What age group are you most drawn to teaching, and why?

question: Why did you choose this particular teacher training course over other routes into teaching?
lookingFor: Evidence the applicant understands the different routes into teaching and has a specific, researched reason for this one.

bullets: Show awareness of alternative routes such as school-led training or apprenticeship models
Name something specific about this course's structure, placements, or mentoring
Connect the choice to how you personally learn best
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at a school-led route as well, but I decided against it because I wanted more time in a university setting engaging with educational theory before I am fully responsible for a class. This course's structure, with a placement in the first term followed by a longer block in the second year, means I get to test what I am learning in the seminar room almost immediately in a real classroom. I also spoke to a current student at an open day who described how closely the subject tutors work with the placement mentors, which matters to me because I learn best when theory and practice are actually joined up rather than taught separately. That combination is why this course specifically made sense for me.

commonMistakes: Not knowing that alternative routes into teaching exist
Praise so generic it could apply to any training provider
No connection between the course structure and how the applicant learns
followUps: What would you do if theory and placement experience seemed to contradict each other?

question: What first got you interested in education as a field, rather than just a career you drifted into?
lookingFor: A specific, credible origin story rather than a rehearsed answer with no personal detail.

bullets: Point to a specific person, class, or event that sparked the interest
Explain what stayed with you about it, not just what happened
Show the interest has developed since then rather than staying static
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It started with a teacher I had in year nine who noticed I was struggling with maths anxiety rather than maths itself, and quietly restructured how she questioned me in class so I could answer without the whole room watching me freeze. I did not have language for it then, but I remember thinking that she had solved a problem that was not really about the subject at all. That stuck with me, and when I started reading about pedagogy for my extended project a few years later I realised what she had done had a name, differentiation, and that it was something you could actually study and get better at. That was the point it stopped being a nice memory and became something I wanted to do myself.

commonMistakes: A generic 'I've always loved kids' with no specific memory
An answer with no connection to how the interest grew over time
Sounding like it was decided for them rather than chosen
followUps: Have you had any experiences since then that changed or challenged that early view?

question: Tell us about a time you have spent in a classroom or with a group of children. What did you learn from it?
lookingFor: Concrete, reflective experience in an educational setting with a genuine takeaway, not just a list of hours completed.

bullets: Describe a specific placement, volunteering role, or classroom observation
Focus on one moment or realisation rather than summarising the whole experience
Show what it taught you about teaching that you did not expect
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I spent two weeks observing a year four class before applying, and the thing that surprised me most was how much of the teacher's actual skill was invisible if you were not looking for it, things like the timing of when she moved around the room or how she used silence to settle a noisy transition. I had expected teaching to be mostly about explaining content clearly, but I left thinking it is at least as much about managing attention and energy in a room of thirty different children at once. That changed what I am looking for from this course, because I now want just as much focus on behaviour and classroom management as on subject pedagogy.

commonMistakes: Listing hours or placements with no specific reflection
Describing the experience but not what it changed in their thinking
Overstating responsibility they did not actually have
followUps: What would you have done differently if you had been leading that class yourself?

question: Has any book or piece of educational research shaped how you think about teaching?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine engagement with education theory beyond the reading list, including the ability to critique it, not just name-drop it.

bullets: Name a specific book, study, or theorist and summarise the actual idea accurately
Explain how it changed or confirmed something in your own thinking
Show some critical distance, not just uncritical praise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Dylan Wiliam's work on formative assessment last year, and the idea that stuck with me is that feedback only actually helps learning if it changes what the pupil does next, not just how they feel about the work. It made me rethink something I had seen during my volunteering, where teachers wrote long comments on essays that pupils barely read past the grade. I am not sure his approach translates perfectly to every subject, especially something as open-ended as art, but the underlying principle that assessment should drive action rather than just measure it has genuinely changed how I think about giving feedback.

commonMistakes: Naming a book or theorist without being able to explain the actual idea
No personal reflection connecting it to their own experience
Treating the theory as unquestionable rather than engaging critically
followUps: Can you think of a situation where that idea might not apply?

question: What do you understand by the term 'differentiation' in teaching, and why does it matter?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate grasp of a core pedagogical concept with a concrete example, not just a dictionary definition.

bullets: Define differentiation as adapting teaching to different pupils' needs and starting points
Give a concrete example of how it might work in practice
Explain why a single approach for a whole class usually fails some pupils
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Differentiation means adjusting the task, the support, or the way you explain something so that pupils at different starting points can all make progress from the same lesson, rather than teaching to one imagined average pupil. In the placement I observed, the teacher gave the same core word problem to the whole class but offered different scaffolding, a visual number line for some pupils and an open version with larger numbers for others who needed a challenge. It matters because a class of thirty pupils will never actually be at the same point in their understanding, so treating them as if they were means you either lose the pupils who are behind or bore the ones who are ahead.

commonMistakes: Confusing differentiation with simply giving different pupils different grades
A definition with no concrete classroom example
Assuming differentiation only applies to lower-ability pupils, not stretch
followUps: What are the risks of differentiating badly?

question: A pupil is being consistently disruptive in a lesson you are teaching on placement. Walk us through how you would handle it.
lookingFor: A structured, realistic approach that starts with low-level strategies and escalates appropriately, showing awareness of the pupil's dignity and the rest of the class.

bullets: Start with the least intrusive strategy that keeps the lesson moving for everyone else
Address the pupil privately rather than confronting them publicly
Show awareness that disruption often has an underlying cause worth understanding
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first move would be something low-key, moving physically closer to the pupil while continuing to teach, or a quiet non-verbal cue, because calling attention to it in front of the class often makes a pupil dig in rather than settle. If it continued, I would speak to them briefly and privately, maybe while the class is working independently, rather than stopping the whole lesson to address it. I would also want to find out afterwards whether something specific was going on, since I have seen on placement that disruption is sometimes a pupil covering for not understanding the work rather than pure defiance. If it kept happening I would follow the school's behaviour policy and loop in my mentor, because consistency with the wider system matters more than me solving it alone in the moment.

commonMistakes: Jumping straight to punishment without trying lower-level strategies first
Confronting the pupil publicly in a way that escalates the situation
Ignoring the possibility of an underlying cause for the behaviour
followUps: What would you do if the same pupil disrupted every single lesson that week?

question: How would you make sure a pupil with special educational needs feels included in your classroom?
lookingFor: Practical, informed thinking about inclusion that goes beyond good intentions, showing some real knowledge of how support is actually organised.

bullets: Mention working with existing support, such as an EHC plan, TA, or SENCO, rather than improvising alone
Give a concrete classroom adjustment, not just a general attitude of kindness
Balance individual support with genuinely including the pupil in whole-class activities
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would start by actually reading whatever support plan exists for that pupil and talking to the SENCO or teaching assistant who knows them, rather than assuming I know best from a couple of lessons. On placement I worked with a pupil who had dyslexia, and small changes like providing instructions in writing as well as out loud, and giving slightly more processing time before expecting a hand up, made a real difference without singling him out. What mattered most, though, was making sure those adjustments happened quietly within the normal flow of the lesson rather than in a way that marked him out as different from everyone else, because inclusion that draws attention to itself can end up feeling like exclusion.

commonMistakes: Vague talk of 'treating everyone the same' which is not actually inclusive
No mention of working with existing support staff or plans
Adjustments that inadvertently single the pupil out
followUps: How would you balance that pupil's needs against the needs of the rest of the class?

question: Can you explain what Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is, and how it might shape a lesson?
lookingFor: An accurate grasp of a key developmental theory with a genuine attempt to apply it, not just recited definitions.

bullets: Define the zone of proximal development as the gap between what a pupil can do alone and what they can do with support
Connect it to the idea of scaffolding
Give a practical example of applying it in a lesson
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development is the space between what a pupil can already do independently and what they can achieve with help from a teacher or a more capable peer. The teaching implication is scaffolding, giving just enough support that a pupil can succeed at something slightly beyond their current level, and then gradually removing that support as they become more confident. I saw this in practice on placement in a science lesson, where the teacher modelled the first two steps of a method herself, had pupils attempt the next two with a partner, and only then asked them to complete a similar problem fully independently. It struck me as a much more deliberate structure than just explaining once and setting pupils loose.

commonMistakes: Confusing the zone of proximal development with simple differentiation
Naming the theorist with no accurate account of the idea
No practical classroom example
followUps: What might go wrong if a teacher provided too much scaffolding for too long?

question: What is your view on the growing use of technology, such as tablets or AI tools, in schools?
lookingFor: A balanced, informed opinion showing awareness of both the potential benefits and the genuine risks, not a one-sided cheerleading or dismissal.

bullets: Acknowledge a real benefit, such as personalised practice or access for pupils with additional needs
Acknowledge a real risk, such as over-reliance, screen time, or unequal access at home
Land on a considered, not extreme, position
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think technology has a genuinely useful place, especially for things like adaptive practice tools that can give a pupil more repetition at exactly their level than a teacher managing thirty pupils could realistically provide one on one. But I am cautious about tools like AI writing assistants in particular, because I have read reports of pupils using them to shortcut the actual thinking a piece of writing is meant to develop, and that worries me more than calculators ever did in maths. My view is that technology works best as something the teacher deliberately chooses for a specific purpose in a lesson, rather than something used constantly by default, and I would want to be thoughtful about when I reach for it rather than assuming more technology is automatically better.

commonMistakes: An entirely uncritical, technology-is-great answer
An entirely dismissive, technology-is-bad answer with no nuance
No awareness of unequal access to devices outside school
followUps: How would you handle a pupil using an AI tool to write their homework for them?

question: What is the difference between formative and summative assessment?
lookingFor: A clear distinction between the two with an example of each and a sense of why both matter.

bullets: Define formative assessment as ongoing, used to guide next steps in learning
Define summative assessment as a final judgement of what has been learned, like an exam
Give one classroom example of each
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Formative assessment happens during learning and is meant to inform what happens next, things like a quick quiz at the start of a lesson or a teacher circulating and checking whiteboards mid-task, so you can adjust the lesson in real time. Summative assessment is a judgement made at the end of a unit or course about what has actually been learned, like a term exam or a final piece of coursework, and it is usually recorded as a grade. Both matter, but I think formative assessment is where the actual teaching skill lives, because it is the difference between finding out a pupil is confused today, when you can still do something about it, and finding out three months later on an exam paper when the moment has passed.

commonMistakes: Confusing the two terms or using them interchangeably
Giving definitions but no concrete example
Suggesting one type of assessment is unimportant
followUps: How might you use formative assessment in a single lesson?

question: How would you handle a parent who is unhappy with how their child is being taught or graded?
lookingFor: A calm, professional approach that listens genuinely before responding, and understands the limits of a trainee's own authority.

bullets: Start by listening properly to understand the actual concern before responding
Stay calm and professional even if the criticism feels unfair
Know when to involve a mentor or senior colleague rather than resolving everything alone
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would want to actually hear the parent out first, because what sounds like a complaint about grading is often really about the parent worrying their child is falling behind, and those need different responses. I would try to explain clearly and specifically what the grading was based on, using actual examples from the work rather than getting defensive. As a trainee I would also be honest that I might need to bring in my mentor or the class teacher, particularly if it touched on something like a formal grade boundary or a pattern across a whole term, because I do not think it would be right to promise changes that are not really mine to make.

commonMistakes: Getting defensive rather than listening first
Overpromising changes that are beyond a trainee's authority
No mention of involving a mentor or more senior colleague when appropriate
followUps: What would you do if the parent's complaint felt unreasonable to you personally?

question: In one or two sentences, what do you think good teaching actually looks like?
lookingFor: A concise, genuine articulation of a teaching philosophy that reflects real thought, not a borrowed slogan.

bullets: State a clear, specific view rather than something vague like 'inspiring pupils'
Ground it in an experience or piece of reading that led you to that view
Show awareness that it is a working view, open to revision
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think good teaching is mostly about making it safe for a pupil to be wrong out loud, because that is the moment real learning becomes visible and correctable. That comes partly from watching a teacher on placement who responded to an incorrect answer by saying 'tell me how you got there' instead of just moving to the next pupil, which turned a mistake into useful information for the whole class rather than something to be embarrassed about. I know that is not the whole picture of good teaching, subject knowledge and planning matter enormously too, but it is the part I keep coming back to as the thing that actually changes whether pupils take risks in their learning.

commonMistakes: A vague slogan like 'making learning fun' with no substance
An answer with no personal grounding or example
Presenting the view as a finished, unquestionable truth
followUps: Has anything you have seen on placement challenged that view?

question: Tell us about a time a child or young person you were working with did not respond well to you. What did you do?
lookingFor: Honest reflection on a genuine difficulty, showing self-awareness and a concrete change in approach rather than blaming the child.

bullets: Describe a specific, real situation rather than a hypothetical or invented one
Take ownership of what you could have done differently
Show the concrete change you made and whether it helped
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: During my volunteering at a homework club, there was a boy who would go quiet and disengage whenever I tried to help him with reading, and at first I assumed he just was not interested. It took a while to realise that my habit of jumping in to correct him the moment he mispronounced a word was making him too anxious to keep trying. Once I noticed that, I changed my approach and let him finish a sentence before offering any correction at all, and his willingness to keep going improved noticeably within a couple of sessions. It taught me that what looks like disengagement is often a reaction to something specific I am doing, not just a fixed trait of the pupil.

commonMistakes: Blaming the child's attitude with no self-reflection
Choosing an example with no real difficulty in it
No concrete change described, just a vague 'I tried harder'
followUps: How do you know your explanation for what was going on was actually correct?

question: What do you understand by 'growth mindset', and do you think it is oversold in schools?
lookingFor: Accurate understanding of the concept plus the willingness to critique a popular idea rather than repeat it uncritically.

bullets: Define growth mindset accurately as the belief that ability can develop through effort and strategy
Acknowledge a genuine criticism, such as posters and slogans without changed practice
Land on a considered view of where it actually helps
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Growth mindset, as Carol Dweck described it, is the belief that ability is something that develops through effort and the right strategies, rather than being fixed from birth, and that belief shapes how pupils respond to setbacks. I do think it gets oversold sometimes, schools putting up posters saying 'mistakes help you grow' without actually changing how mistakes are responded to in the classroom, which risks it becoming a slogan rather than a practice. Where I think it genuinely helps is in specific moments, like a teacher praising the strategy a pupil used rather than just calling them clever, because that keeps the pupil's sense of ability tied to something they can actually control.

commonMistakes: Reciting the concept with no critical distance
Dismissing the whole idea without acknowledging any value
Confusing growth mindset with simply praising effort regardless of quality
followUps: Can you give an example of praise that undermines a growth mindset?

question: How would you make sure your teaching reflects and respects a diverse classroom?
lookingFor: Practical, specific thinking about representation and fairness, not just a general statement of good values.

bullets: Give a concrete example, such as diversifying examples, texts, or materials used
Show awareness that fairness sometimes means treating pupils differently, not identically
Avoid treating this as a solved, one-off task rather than ongoing practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: One concrete thing I would do is actually look at whose names, examples, and images appear in the materials I use, because if every worked example in a maths worksheet features the same kind of name or background, that sends a quiet signal about who maths is for. I would also want to be careful about assuming equity means treating every pupil identically, since a pupil who has English as an additional language might genuinely need more time or visual support to access the same task fairly. I do not think this is something you solve once and move on from, it is more like a habit of checking your own materials and assumptions regularly, which is something I would want feedback on from my mentor rather than assuming I am getting right by instinct.

commonMistakes: A statement of values with no concrete practice attached
Assuming equal treatment and fair treatment are always the same thing
Treating diversity as a box to tick rather than an ongoing practice
followUps: Can you think of a time diversity was handled badly in a classroom you observed?

question: A pupil says something to you during a lesson that makes you worried about their safety at home. What would you do?
lookingFor: Clear understanding that safeguarding concerns must be escalated through proper channels immediately, not investigated or kept confidential by the trainee.

bullets: Never promise the pupil confidentiality if what they say raises a safeguarding concern
Record what was said as accurately as possible, without leading questions
Report it immediately to the designated safeguarding lead, not handle it independently
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I would do is listen calmly and not react in a way that shuts the pupil down, but I would also be careful never to promise I would keep it a secret, because I would need to be honest that I have to pass this on to someone who can help. I would avoid asking leading questions and just let them tell me in their own words, writing down what was actually said as soon as possible afterwards rather than relying on memory later. Then I would report it straight to the school's designated safeguarding lead following the school's procedure, because this is not something a trainee should investigate or sit on alone, even with good intentions.

commonMistakes: Promising the pupil confidentiality
Deciding to handle it personally rather than escalating immediately
Asking leading or investigative questions rather than listening
followUps: What would you do if you were not sure whether what was said actually warranted a safeguarding referral?

question: How do you go about reflecting on and improving a lesson after it has not gone well?
lookingFor: A structured, honest approach to self-evaluation that leads to a specific change, not vague self-criticism.

bullets: Separate what actually happened from how it felt in the moment
Identify one or two specific, changeable causes rather than a general sense of failure
Describe a concrete adjustment made for next time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I try to write down what actually happened before I let myself judge it, because in the moment a lesson that went badly can feel like a personal failure when the real cause is something narrow and fixable, like pacing or instructions that were not clear enough. After a lesson on placement where half the class finished a task in five minutes and the rest took twenty, I realised the issue was that I had not built in an extension task, not that the lesson itself was badly planned. The next lesson I built in a 'if you finish early' extension from the start, and it solved that specific problem, which felt more useful than a vague resolution to 'plan better' next time.

commonMistakes: Vague self-criticism with no specific, actionable cause identified
Blaming the pupils entirely for a lesson not going well
No follow-through describing what actually changed afterwards
followUps: How do you make sure you are being honest with yourself rather than making excuses?

question: How would you explain a concept from your subject to a pupil who is struggling, in a way that is different from how you would explain it to an adult?
lookingFor: Genuine subject knowledge combined with the ability to translate it, showing awareness that simplification is a skill, not just using easier words.

bullets: Choose a real concept and show you actually understand it well enough to simplify accurately
Use a concrete analogy or model appropriate to the age group, not just simpler vocabulary
Show awareness of common misconceptions at that age
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If I were explaining fractions to a year four pupil struggling with the idea that a bigger denominator means a smaller piece, I would not start with the abstract rule, I would use a shared pizza, showing that cutting it into eight slices instead of four means each slice is smaller even though eight is the bigger number. I know from reading about common misconceptions that pupils often assume bigger numbers always mean bigger amounts, so I would deliberately pick an example that puts that assumption under pressure rather than avoiding it. To an adult I might just state the rule directly, but with a pupil the goal is building the intuition first and only attaching the formal rule once the picture makes sense to them.

commonMistakes: Just using simpler words without actually adapting the explanation itself
Choosing an analogy that does not actually match the underlying concept
No awareness of typical misconceptions pupils have at that age
followUps: What would you do if the pupil still did not understand after that explanation?

question: Teaching involves working closely with other staff, from teaching assistants to your mentor. Tell us about a time you worked well as part of a team.
lookingFor: A concrete example of collaborative work with a clear outcome, showing you understand teaching is not a solo activity.

bullets: Describe a specific team situation, ideally in an educational or similar setting
Show what you personally contributed, not just what the team achieved
Reflect on what made the collaboration work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Running the homework club, I worked alongside two other volunteers each week, and we found early on that we were duplicating effort by all trying to help the same handful of vocal pupils. We started a quick two-minute check-in before each session to divide up who would focus on which pupils, based on who each of us had built a rapport with already. It sounds small, but it meant quieter pupils who used to get overlooked actually got consistent attention, and the session ran far more smoothly. What made it work was that we were willing to say out loud what was not working rather than just muddling along.

commonMistakes: An example where the applicant worked entirely alone
No specific personal contribution described
No reflection on what actually made the collaboration effective
followUps: What would you do if you disagreed with your mentor's approach to something?

question: What do you understand about how the curriculum you would be teaching is structured, and have you looked at it closely?
lookingFor: Evidence of actual research into the relevant curriculum framework, not a vague awareness that one exists.

bullets: Show familiarity with the actual structure, such as key stages or subject programmes of study
Mention a specific detail that shows genuine reading, not surface knowledge
Connect it to how it would shape planning
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I have gone through the primary national curriculum programmes of study for English and maths in some detail, since that is the phase I want to train in, and what struck me was how much more specific key stage two objectives are compared to what I remembered from being a pupil myself, right down to expectations around specific grammatical terms pupils should be able to use by a certain year. I think understanding that structure matters for planning because it tells you not just what to teach but roughly what a pupil should already be able to do coming in, which shapes how much scaffolding a lesson actually needs. I know this is something I will get much more familiar with once I am actually planning lessons, but I wanted to go in with a real sense of the framework rather than learning it entirely on the job.

commonMistakes: Vague awareness that a curriculum exists with no specific detail
Confusing the curriculum with exam board specifications where not relevant
No connection made to how it would actually affect planning
followUps: What surprised you most when you actually read through it?

question: A pupil in your class is consistently falling behind despite seeming to try hard. How would you approach this?
lookingFor: A methodical, empathetic approach that investigates the cause before jumping to a fix, and involves the wider support system.

bullets: Investigate possible causes rather than assuming laziness or low ability
Involve appropriate support, such as the SENCO or the pupil's other teachers
Describe a specific adjustment to try, framed as something to monitor rather than a guaranteed fix
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The fact that they are trying hard and still falling behind would make me want to rule out something specific getting in the way, rather than assuming it is just about ability, so I would look at their work over a few weeks to see if the difficulty is consistent across topics or concentrated somewhere specific. I would also talk to other teachers who see them, and if a pattern suggested something like an undiagnosed learning difficulty, I would raise it with the SENCO rather than trying to diagnose it myself. In the meantime I would try a small, specific adjustment, like breaking instructions into smaller written steps, and actually track whether it made a measurable difference rather than just assuming it helped.

commonMistakes: Assuming the pupil simply is not trying hard enough despite the premise
No involvement of other staff or support structures
A vague plan with no way of checking whether it actually helped
followUps: What would you say to the pupil themselves about their progress?

question: Teaching is widely known to be demanding, with heavy workload and emotional strain. What makes you confident you can sustain that?
lookingFor: A realistic understanding of the demands of the job, backed by some evidence the applicant has already coped with sustained pressure.

bullets: Show realistic awareness of the demands, not a naive dismissal of them
Point to a specific past experience of managing sustained pressure well
Mention a genuine strategy for managing workload or stress, not just 'I'll cope'
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I do not think I am under any illusion that this will be easy, I have read about workload surveys and spoken to two teachers I know about the marking and planning that happens outside contact hours, and it is a lot. What gives me some confidence is that I have managed sustained pressure before, juggling A levels with a part time job and the volunteering I mentioned, and what got me through that was being disciplined about planning my week rather than just reacting to whatever felt most urgent each day. I also know from talking to those teachers that building a small support network of colleagues you can be honest with matters a lot, and that is something I would actively look to do rather than assume I can manage entirely on my own.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the difficulty of the job as overstated
No concrete past experience of managing pressure
A strategy that amounts to just 'working harder' with no actual plan
followUps: What would you do in a week where the workload genuinely felt unmanageable?

question: Teacher training involves a lot of group work and peer discussion with your cohort. What would you bring to that?
lookingFor: A specific, credible sense of what the applicant offers a cohort, beyond generic enthusiasm.

bullets: Name a specific perspective, experience, or skill you would bring
Show awareness that a cohort benefits from disagreement and challenge, not just agreement
Avoid sounding like you expect to only take from the group and not contribute
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Having volunteered specifically with pupils who had English as an additional language, I think I would bring a perspective on language and access that not everyone in a general cohort discussion might raise unprompted, and I would want to push discussions to actually consider it rather than assume a strategy works the same for every pupil. I also do not mind being the person who asks the slightly awkward question in a seminar, like whether a strategy we are being taught actually holds up outside the ideal classroom it is usually described in, because I think cohorts learn more from a bit of honest pushback than from everyone nodding along. I would want that to go both ways, and take genuine challenge from others just as readily as I would offer it.

commonMistakes: A generic answer like 'I am a good listener' with no real substance
Describing only what they hope to get from the cohort, not give
Overstating expertise they do not actually have yet
followUps: Can you think of a time you changed your mind because of a peer's challenge?

question: Where do you see yourself in your teaching career in ten years, and how does this course get you started on that path?
lookingFor: A grounded, honest sense of direction that connects to the course without sounding either aimless or over-rehearsed.

bullets: Give a direction rather than an overly precise job title
Connect it honestly to what this specific course offers as a starting point
Show openness to the path changing as experience accumulates
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In ten years I would like to be leading on literacy or intervention within a primary school, working specifically with pupils who are falling behind, since that is the part of teaching I already find most compelling in the volunteering I have done. I know that exact role might not exist in the form I am imagining it, and that classroom experience itself might redirect me somewhere I have not considered yet, and I am genuinely fine with that. What I am confident of is that this course, with its strong placement structure, is the right place to build the classroom foundation that any of those directions would need, because none of it means anything without first being a solid classroom teacher.

commonMistakes: An overly specific, unrealistic ten-year plan with no flexibility
A goal disconnected from anything the course actually offers
Sounding uncertain about wanting to stay in teaching at all
followUps: What is the first thing you want to get good at once you are actually teaching your own class?
